name: Mailbird
tagline: Build a Windows email client with unified inbox, local search, and simple integrations

pricing.notes: Typical Standard subscription rate; lifetime options can also exist.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Mailbird, build a Windows email client with unified inbox, local search, and simple integrations. The hard boundary is windows polish, provider compatibility, app integrations, sync, and support, plus mail infrastructure, integrations, and client polish.
coreLoopDIY: Connect existing mailboxes to a Windows email client, index messages locally for fast search, provide a unified focused inbox, and send through each account's normal SMTP service.
whatYouLose: Windows polish, provider compatibility, app integrations, sync, and support
moatNotes: mail infrastructure, integrations, and client polish
ongoingBurden: IMAP quirks, OAuth, MIME, threading, search, attachments, offline sync, notifications, secure storage, and provider changes
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Mailbird because an email client can be rebuilt; operating a trusted mail service with excellent deliverability cannot. The recurring cost buys IMAP quirks, OAuth, MIME, threading, search, attachments, offline sync, notifications, secure storage, and provider changes, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: mailcow
priorArt.desc: Popular open-source mail-server suite that demonstrates the operational complexity of hosted mail.

alternatives.name: BlueMail Personal
alternatives.desc: A free Windows unified inbox with unlimited accounts, search and clusters; integrations are thinner.

alternatives.name: Edison Mail
alternatives.desc: Unified accounts, search and rules on Windows for free; integrations are not the point.

alternatives.name: Mailspring
alternatives.desc: A modern open-source unified inbox for Windows; several workflow niceties remain Pro.

alternatives.name: Spark Free
alternatives.desc: A polished Windows inbox with smart sorting and search; the ecosystem of side-panel apps is gone.

alternatives.name: Thunderbird
alternatives.desc: The sturdy Windows answer with extensions and local search; visual polish varies by decade.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Wino Mail
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Open-source code, but the free Store build sells unlimited accounts; an account-capped unified inbox misses the job.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Standard plan and a personal desktop mail client DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Mailbird in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, SQLite, IMAP, SMTP, and OAuth where available; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: connect existing mailboxes to a Windows email client, index messages locally for fast search, provide a unified focused inbox, and send through each account's normal SMTP service.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Support one IMAP and SMTP account with credentials stored only in the OS keychain.
Index headers and message bodies locally with resumable sync and a visible status page.
Implement standards-based threading, folders, labels, archive, snooze, drafts, and search.
Render HTML email in a locked-down sandbox and block remote images by default.
Send multipart messages with attachments and preserve a local copy of every draft.
Add export, local cache reset, account reconnect, diagnostics, and safe logging.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out running a public mail server.
Deliberately leave out shared team inboxes and sales workflows.
Deliberately leave out mobile push services and provider-scale spam filtering.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
